F1.detail: The commit message's rejection rationale does not re-derive. It says the derived table 'pack[s] the heaviest module into 31 peers where the current entry gives 29'. Under the committed MODULE_WEIGHTS the heaviest module test_sov_fresh.py lands in a bucket of 27 (26 peers), deterministically and independent of any measurement; 29 is merely the largest bucket in that partition and belongs to a different module. The derived side reproduces at 31 (30 peers). The true comparison is 31 vs 27, so the derived table is worse than the record says and the decision not to adopt survives, but the number entered in the permanent record is wrong.

F2.detail: The --failfast case in sov_tooling_verdict.verdict_defects is now vacuous. At b1448ee the runner parsed no argv, so --failfast was ignored, the miniature tree really ran, the failing module really refused, and the case observed exit 1 from the runner's own verdict path. At bd94865 the new argparse rejects the unknown flag with exit 2 before a single module is loaded; the case still sees non-zero, still passes, and now grades argparse's usage error instead of the runner's verdict. Proven: candidate rc=2, stderr 'unrecognized arguments: --failfast', no module executed, failure marker absent; base rc=1 with the marker present. This is the repository's named defect class -- a check that no longer reads the bytes it grades -- introduced by this commit and not reported in it. The other three cases still genuinely grade the runner, so the check would still catch a runner that swallowed shard failures.

F3.detail: The new cost reading is never compared against the module population it is a reading of. run_tooling_tests.main now holds both len(modules) and len(costs) and prints both lines adjacent to each other, and grades neither. Demonstrated with 12 modules where one exits its shard process with status 0 at import: the runner prints '== tooling cost: 9 modules, 4 shards ==' immediately above 'PASS: repository tooling tests (12 modules, 4 shards)' and exits 0, with three modules never run. The swallow itself is pre-existing and identical at base (R1); what is new is that this change is the first to hold the evidence that would refuse it and chooses to declare rather than measure. A single equality between the two counts would convert a silent PASS into a refusal.

F4.detail: The driver computes and prints a per-module PASS/FAIL token on every COST_MODULE line, and no consumer ever reads it. module_costs reads only parts[1] and parts[2]; main filters every COST_MODULE-prefixed line out of the shard log before printing. The per-module verdict is therefore serialised and discarded, and the cost report lists a failing module's seconds indistinguishably from a passing one's -- confirmed in the 'one failing among five passing' probe, whose cost section reads only '0.006s (6 module(s) under 1.000s)'. A token that looks authoritative in a log and is read by nobody is the shape the repository's own history warns about.

F5.detail: test_a_loader_that_raises_refuses_one_module_and_not_the_whole_shard restores behaviour but leaks state. It assigns and restores an INSTANCE attribute on the process-wide unittest.defaultTestLoader singleton. Before the module runs, 'loadTestsFromName' is not in vars(unittest.defaultTestLoader); after it runs, it is, holding the correct bound method. Calls behave identically, and the 14 modules that run after it in shard 4 all pass, so there is no live consequence. The consequence that exists is silent shadowing: a later class-level patch of unittest.TestLoader.loadTestsFromName is invisible through defaultTestLoader after this test has run -- proven to read False where it reads True beforehand. unittest.mock.patch.object restores by deleting the attribute and does not leave the residue.

F6.detail: The 'preserves the existing isolation' claim needs one qualifier. Process isolation is preserved exactly: still one subprocess per shard, still all of a shard's modules in one interpreter. Load-order isolation is not identical. python -m unittest a b c imports every named module before running any test; the driver imports module N+1 only after module N's tests have finished, so import-time state (cwd, environment, sys.modules) is now exposed to the preceding module's test side effects in a way it was not. No module among the 111 is affected today -- all pass, and per-module counts are identical for all 110 unchanged modules -- so the claim holds empirically. The wording is stronger than what was measured.

F7.detail: Two of the eight new cases call driver.run_module('test_sov_kernel'), so test_sov_kernel's 23 tests execute three times per suite run: once as its own module and twice nested inside test_run_tooling_tests. The nested runtime is attributed to test_run_tooling_tests by the very instrument this change adds. The amount is small here (test_sov_kernel measures 0.004s) but the cost reader's own module is the one that misattributes, which is the defect the change exists to remove.

F8.detail: The commit message says 'Three tests here named test_sov_branch directly'. The diff shows three hardcodes removed, but only two named test_sov_branch.py; the third, in test_full_corpus_reader_gets_fewer_peers_than_default_modules, named test_sov_docs.py. The count is right and the repair is right; the module named in the record is not.

R4 trap T2 applies: verify exit 0 is not conformance. 46 declared conformance defeating fixtures report FAIL at both revisions, an identical count; this change touches none of them.

R5 the tooling check runs at 15.3-16.3s pooled inside verify and 12.6-12.9s isolated on this host, so it remains below the 30.000s catastrophic ceiling in contracts/verification-budget.json by a wide margin, and this change does not move it toward that ceiling. It remains the largest single budget overrun in the suite at both revisions.

R6 no defeating fixture exists for the cost reading itself. The new tests grade the parser (module_costs), the derivation (measured_weights) and the loader guard, but nothing proves a reported number corresponds to real elapsed work: the two behavioural cases assert only seconds >= 0.0 and seconds > 0.0. The cost report is therefore reported-but-unwitnessed output, which is admissible for a scheduling hint and would not be for a gate.
